claims.text: Template-assisted dealloying can produce noble metal–based high-entropy alloy three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
Using a predesigned sacrificial template enhances atomic-scale compositional control in NM-HEAs.
Low-temperature controlled etching increases the catalytically active surface area of NM-HEA nanoframeworks.
Conventional synthesis methods produce noble metal–based HEA bulk forms or nanoparticles with diverse compositions and complex surface structures.
A sacrificial template can be integrated into an NM-HEA precursor and selectively removed by low-temperature chemical etching.
The etching environment can preserve the noble-metal matrix while removing the sacrificial template.
A predesigned sacrificial template directs the locations of nucleation and dealloying sites.
Directing nucleation and dealloying sites enables formation of an interconnected three-dimensional framework.
Selective removal of labile elements or sacrificial components forms a porous, interconnected nanoframework.
Template-assisted dealloying permits atomic-scale adjustment of the remaining noble-metal matrix.
The resulting nanoframework exposes more catalytic active sites.
Controlled and uniform porosity increases active-site density and improves catalytic effectiveness.
Template-assisted dealloying produces a more homogeneous atomic composition than conventional bulk or nanoparticle fusion methods.
Traditional melting, mechanical alloying, and spark plasma sintering provide less atomic-level structural control and less three-dimensional porosity.
The effectiveness of template-assisted dealloying depends on the noble-metal composition and sacrificial-template design.
Very high reaction temperatures may damage nanoframework integrity.
The attainable atomic precision and catalytic enhancement remain uncertain because synthesis–structure–property relationships in high-entropy nanoalloys are not fully understood.
